source_refs.note: Compound ions: a main subheading of 10.2.2 Finding the oxidation number of an element in a compound or a radical, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 215-216.

blocks.text: Compound ions are ions with two or more different atoms. Examples are the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, and the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻.
Calculate the oxidation number (Ox. No.) of sulphur in SO₄²⁻.
[Ox. No. of S] + 4 [Ox. No. of O] = -2
Thus, the oxidation number of sulphur in SO₄²⁻ is +6.
Calculate the oxidation number (Ox. No.) of manganese in KMnO₄.
(Ox. No. of K) + (Ox. No. of Mn) + 4 (Ox. No. of O) = 0
Thus, the oxidation number (Ox. No.) of Mn in KMnO₄ is + 7.

blocks.prompt: a) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer with examples.
blocks.explanation:
Oxidation is the loss of electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
Reduction is the gain of electrons: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

blocks.prompt: b) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of change in oxidation number with examples.
blocks.explanation:
Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ (+2 to +3).
Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number: Cl₂ → Cl⁻ (0 to −1).

blocks.prompt:
c) Determine Ox. No. of:
i) Oxygen (N) in Na₂O
ii) Iodine (I) in ICl₃
iii) Nitrogen (N) in NO₃¹⁻
iv) Chromium (Cr) in K₂Cr₂O₇
blocks.explanation:
i) Na₂O: 2(+1) + O = 0, so O = −2.
ii) ICl₃: Cl is more electronegative (−1): I + 3(−1) = 0, so I = +3.
iii) NO₃⁻: N + 3(−2) = −1, so N = +5.
iv) K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(−2) = 0, so 2Cr = +12 and Cr = +6.

blocks.text: Quick Check 10.1 c (i) prints “Oxygen (N) in Na₂O”; the symbol of oxygen is O, so it should read Oxygen (O) in Na₂O.
